POLYGRAPH AND LIE DETECTOR TEST PROHIBITION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's statutory prohibition on polygraph and lie detector testing of job applicants and employees, codified at California Labor Code § 432.2, as it relates to Acme, Inc. It states facts about what California law prohibits, permits, and requires in this area. It is not itself a testing policy, a consent form, or a determination that any particular test, request, or examination involving Jordan Lee does or does not comply with this law, and it does not tell Jordan Lee or Acme, Inc. what to do about any particular hiring or employment decision.

CORE PROHIBITION ON POLYGRAPH AND LIE DETECTOR TESTS
California law prohibits an employer from demanding or requiring an applicant for employment or prospective employment, or an employee, to submit to or take a polygraph, lie detector, or similar test or examination as a condition of employment or continued employment. The statute applies to both stages of the employment relationship it names: the hiring stage ("applicant for employment or prospective employment") and ongoing employment ("employee"). The prohibition is stated as a blanket rule tied to any test used "as a condition of employment or continued employment" — the statute's own text does not limit it to any particular industry, job type, or reason the employer might want the test administered.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "No employer shall demand or require any applicant for employment or prospective employment or any employee to submit to or take a polygraph, lie detector or similar test or examination as a condition of employment or continued employment."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 432.2, subd. (a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, prohibition on polygraph and lie detector tests as a condition of employment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.2.)
  Known gap: This is California law only, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. A separate federal statute, the Employee Polygraph Protection Act, imposes an overlapping but not identical prohibition on many employers nationwide, addressed in a later clause of this document. This clause states the general rule; a following clause addresses a specific, textual exception within this same statutory section for government employers, and another addresses a separate written-notice obligation the same section imposes when a test is requested rather than demanded or required. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific test, request, or examination.

EXCEPTION FOR FEDERAL, STATE, AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT EMPLOYERS
The same statutory sentence that states the prohibition also states its own express exception: the prohibition does not apply to the federal government or any of its agencies, or to state government or any of its agencies or local subdivisions, including counties, cities and counties, cities, districts, authorities, and agencies. In other words, on the text of this section, government employers at every level named — federal, state, and local — are excluded from this particular prohibition; a private employer is not.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "The prohibition of this section does not apply to the federal government or any agency thereof or the state government or any agency or local subdivision thereof, including, but not limited to, counties, cities and counties, cities, districts, authorities, and agencies."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 432.2, subd. (a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, government-employer exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.2.)
  Known gap: This exception is part of the same sentence and the same subdivision (a) of Labor Code § 432.2 as the core prohibition in the previous clause — it is not an independent source, but the second half of the same statutory text already quoted there. This is a genuine, textual carve-out worth flagging on its own: a reader assuming this statute reaches every employer in California without exception would be assuming something the statute's own text does not say. This document does not address whether some other statute, regulation, or constitutional provision might separately restrict polygraph or lie detector testing by a government employer; it addresses only the specific exception written into this section. This is California law only, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation, and not a claim about how any other state treats government employers. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any particular employer falls within this exception.

WRITTEN NOTICE OF RIGHTS BEFORE A REQUESTED TEST
A separate subdivision of the same statute addresses a situation distinct from demanding or requiring a test: an employer requesting that a person take such a test, or administering one. In that situation, the statute prohibits the employer from requesting or administering the test without first advising the person, in writing, at the time the test is to be administered, of the rights the statute guarantees. On the statute's own structure, subdivision (a)'s prohibition on demanding or requiring a test as a condition of employment is an absolute bar with only the government-employer exception described elsewhere in this document; subdivision (b)'s written-notice obligation is a separate, narrower rule addressing a request for, or administration of, a test that is not being demanded or required as a condition of employment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "No employer shall request any person to take such a test, or administer such a test, without first advising the person in writing at the time the test is to be administered of the rights guaranteed by this section."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 432.2, subd. (b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, written notice of statutory rights before a requested or administered test (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=432.2.)
  Known gap: This clause states subdivision (b) of the same Labor Code § 432.2 already quoted in the two preceding clauses — all three clauses draw on the same single statutory section, not independent corroborating sources. The statute's text does not itself define what "advising the person in writing... of the rights guaranteed by this section" must specifically say beyond referencing those statutory rights, and this document does not attempt to supply model notice language. This is California law only, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. This document is informational only: it does not itself constitute the written notice this subdivision describes, and does not determine whether any particular request for, or administration of, a test complies with it.

MISDEMEANOR PENALTY FOR VIOLATION
A separately numbered section of the same statutory article — the article covering contracts and applications for employment, which includes the polygraph and lie detector prohibition described elsewhere in this document — makes a violation of any provision of that article a misdemeanor. On its text, this penalty provision is not limited to the polygraph and lie detector section specifically; it applies to "this article" as a whole, meaning it also covers violations of the other, separately numbered sections within the same article on contracts and applications for employment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Any person violating this article is guilty of a misdemeanor."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 433 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, misdemeanor penalty for violation of the article (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=433.)
  Known gap: This is a genuinely separate, independently numbered statutory section (Labor Code § 433) from Labor Code § 432.2 cited in the preceding clauses, appearing in the same statutory article rather than as a subdivision of the same section — it is treated here as an independently verified source, not as a restatement of § 432.2's own text. Because § 433 penalizes violation of the entire article (Labor Code §§ 430–435), it is not specific to polygraph testing by its own terms; this document does not independently verify or describe what other conduct that article covers beyond the polygraph and lie detector provisions already addressed. This document did not locate, and does not describe, any separate civil penalty, administrative remedy, or private right of action specific to § 432.2 within this same article; only this criminal misdemeanor provision was found and confirmed. This is California law only, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation, and not a claim about how any other state penalizes similar conduct. This document is informational only: it does not itself charge, prosecute, or determine guilt of any offense.

COMPARISON TO THE FEDERAL EMPLOYEE POLYGRAPH PROTECTION ACT
Separately from California law, a federal statute — the Employee Polygraph Protection Act — also restricts lie detector testing in employment. Subject to two statutory exceptions found elsewhere in that same federal law, it is unlawful for a covered employer to require, request, suggest, or cause an employee or prospective employee to take or submit to a lie detector test; to use, accept, refer to, or inquire about the results of such a test; or to discharge, discipline, discriminate against, deny employment or promotion to, or threaten any such action against a person who refuses to take the test, based on its results, or for exercising rights under the federal law. This federal prohibition applies to "any employer engaged in or affecting commerce or in the production of goods for commerce," a jurisdictional test grounded in federal commerce-power coverage, rather than the government-employer exception found in the California statute described elsewhere in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "it shall be unlawful for any employer engaged in or affecting commerce or in the production of goods for commerce- (1) directly or indirectly, to require, request, suggest, or cause any employee or prospective employee to take or submit to any lie detector test;"
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2002 (Employee Polygraph Protection Act) (Office of the Law Revision Counsel, U.S. Code text), 29 U.S.C. § 2002, prohibitions on lie detector tests by covered employers (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title29-section2002&num=0&edition=prelim)
  Known gap: This is a separate, independently confirmed federal source (29 U.S.C. § 2002) — not a subdivision of the California Labor Code sections cited elsewhere in this document — genuinely corroborating that a comparable, broader-reaching prohibition also exists at the federal level. The quoted provision itself states that it applies "except as provided in sections 2006 and 2007" of the same federal title; this document did not independently fetch or verify the text of those two referenced exception sections, so their specific scope (which is understood to include certain government employers, security-service and pharmaceutical-manufacturing businesses under ongoing investigations, and related situations) is not confirmed here and should not be assumed to mirror California's own, narrower, government-employer exception. This federal law and the California statute are separate legal regimes that can overlap in their coverage of the same employer; this document does not state which one, if either, would govern any particular reader's situation, and does not attempt to reconcile every difference between them beyond the specific points stated in this clause.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT

Signature: _______________
Date: September 1, 2026

On behalf of Acme, Inc.: _______________
City, State: Oakland, California
